intended_object: For a set S of primes, an additive group (or monoid) A is S-divisible when nA = A for every positive integer n whose prime divisors all lie in S, i.e. for every n ∈ ℕ(S). This is the notion used in Neukirch–Schmidt–Wingberg I §7. Inferred from the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
The body asks that `n • · : A → A` be surjective for every n in `Nat.primeSupportedIndices S`. That set is the submonoid of ℕ generated by the primes in S. The lemma `mem_primeSupportedIndices_iff` proves it is exactly the set of positive n whose prime divisors all lie in S, which is NSW's ℕ(S). So the predicate says nA = A for all n ∈ ℕ(S), which is the textbook definition.

Edge cases behave correctly:
- n = 0 is never in the set, so the predicate does not degenerate.
- For S = ∅ the only index is 1, and the predicate holds trivially.
- For S equal to all primes it is ordinary divisibility.
- `ZMod p` is S-divisible exactly when p ∉ S, as the library proves.

The library also proves that the predicate is equivalent to p•A = A for each p ∈ S.

On generality: it is stated for an arbitrary `AddMonoid`, which is at least as general as the abelian groups or modules in the literature.

On Mathlib: `DivisibleBy A ℕ` requires division by every nonzero natural number and carries a division operation as data. It is the special case where S is all primes, not this notion. Mathlib has no predicate for divisibility restricted to a set of primes.
